claim: Staphylococcus aureus is responsible for hundreds of thousands of severe infections worldwide every year.
source: Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most notorious and widespread bacterial pathogens, responsible for hundreds of thousands of severe infections worldwide every year.
evidence: This is a general statement about the global burden of S. aureus infections, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: MRSA infections increase mortality, morbidity, and hospital stay compared to MSSA infections.
source: Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) poses a particular clinical threat, as MRSA infections increase mortality, morbidity, and hospital stay, as compared to those caused by methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA; Ippolito et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ippolito et al., 2010.

claim: β-lactams inhibit the activity of transpeptidase enzymes during peptidoglycan synthesis in bacterial cell walls.
source: Part of MRSA's notoriety stems from its strong resistance against the β-lactam family of antibiotics, such as penicillins and cephalosporins, which inhibit the activity of transpeptidase enzymes during peptidoglycan synthesis in bacterial cell walls (Tomasz, 1979).
evidence: The mechanism of β-lactam action is supported by citation to Tomasz, 1979.

claim: β-lactams are one of the most commonly prescribed drug classes.
source: β-lactams are one of the most commonly prescribed drug classes, with many designated as 'Critically Important' antimicrobials by the World Health Organization (WHO, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2019.

claim: In 2019, MRSA accounted for more than 100,000 deaths attributable to drug-resistant infections worldwide.
source: Indeed, in 2019, MRSA alone accounted for more than 100,000 deaths attributable to drug-resistant infections worldwide (Murray et al., 2022).
evidence: The mortality statistic is supported by citation to Murray et al., 2022.

claim: The SCCmec cassette is a mobile genetic element that carries the resistance gene mecA.
source: A chief mediator of β-lactams resistance in MRSA is the SCCmec cassette, a mobile genetic element that carries the resistance gene mecA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of MRSA resistance.

claim: MecA encodes for the penicillin-binding protein 2A (PBP2a), a transpeptidase that has a low affinity for β-lactams.
source: MecA encodes for the penicillin-binding protein 2 A (PBP2a), a transpeptidase that has a low affinity for β-lactams (Zapun et al., 2008).
evidence: The function of MecA is supported by citation to Zapun et al., 2008.

claim: PBP2a can participate in peptidoglycan synthesis even in the presence of β-lactams, resulting in cell survival.
source: This lower affinity permits PBP2a to participate in peptidoglycan synthesis even in the presence of β-lactams, ultimately resulting in cell survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established mechanism of PBP2a function.

claim: Numerous MRSA strains carry β-lactamases, such as BlaZ, that degrade β-lactams.
source: In addition to mecA, numerous MRSA strains also carry β-lactamases, such as BlaZ, that degrade β-lactams, thus further contributing to drug resistance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about additional resistance mechanisms in MRSA.

claim: Current clinical treatment options against MRSA rely primarily on vancomycin and daptomycin.
source: Together, these mechanisms can severely limit treatment options against MRSA, with current clinical treatment options relying primarily on vancomycin and daptomycin (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: The treatment options are supported by citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: There is increasing resistance of MRSA to vancomycin and daptomycin.
source: Both vancomycin and daptomycin are last resort antibiotics against MRSA, and a major concern is the increasing resistance of MRSA to these drugs (Turner et al., 2019; Barros et al., 2019).
evidence: The increasing resistance is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2019 and Barros et al., 2019.

claim: Phages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria.
source: Phages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria, posing one of the greatest existential threats to bacterial communities, with some estimates suggesting that 40% of all bacterial mortality worldwide is caused by phage predation (Wilhelm and Suttle, 1999).
evidence: The definition and impact of phages is supported by citation to Wilhelm and Suttle, 1999.

claim: 40% of all bacterial mortality worldwide is caused by phage predation.
source: Phages are viruses that infect and kill bacteria, posing one of the greatest existential threats to bacterial communities, with some estimates suggesting that 40% of all bacterial mortality worldwide is caused by phage predation (Wilhelm and Suttle, 1999).
evidence: The mortality estimate is supported by citation to Wilhelm and Suttle, 1999.

claim: Phages are highly specific to their hosts by reducing off-target killing.
source: Phages offer certain advantages over traditional antibiotics: they are highly specific to their hosts by reducing off-target killing; they self-amplify and evolve, enabling the rapid generation of new phage variants with improved activities; and they are generally regarded as safe, as toxicity has been reported only in extremely rare cases in animals and patients (Kortright et al., 2019).
evidence: The advantages of phages are supported by citation to Kortright et al., 2019.

claim: Phages self-amplify and evolve, enabling the rapid generation of new phage variants with improved activities.
source: Phages offer certain advantages over traditional antibiotics: they are highly specific to their hosts by reducing off-target killing; they self-amplify and evolve, enabling the rapid generation of new phage variants with improved activities; and they are generally regarded as safe, as toxicity has been reported only in extremely rare cases in animals and patients (Kortright et al., 2019).
evidence: The advantages of phages are supported by citation to Kortright et al., 2019.

claim: Phage toxicity has been reported only in extremely rare cases in animals and patients.
source: Phages offer certain advantages over traditional antibiotics: they are highly specific to their hosts by reducing off-target killing; they self-amplify and evolve, enabling the rapid generation of new phage variants with improved activities; and they are generally regarded as safe, as toxicity has been reported only in extremely rare cases in animals and patients (Kortright et al., 2019).
evidence: The safety profile is supported by citation to Kortright et al., 2019.

claim: Over a dozen promising case studies and clinical trials of phage therapy against S. aureus infections have been reported in the past decade.
source: Indeed, against S. aureus infections, over a dozen promising case studies and clinical trials have been reported in the past decade (Hatoum-Aslan, 2021).
evidence: The clinical evidence is supported by citation to Hatoum-Aslan, 2021.

claim: Resistance against phage evolved in 75% of human clinical cases in which the evolution of resistance was monitored.
source: According to one meta-analysis that focused on phage therapy outcomes, resistance against phage evolved in 75% of human clinical cases in which the evolution of resistance was monitored (Oechslin, 2018).
evidence: The resistance statistic is supported by citation to Oechslin, 2018.

claim: Mutations represent a chief pathway by which bacteria evolve resistance against phage.
source: Mutations represent a chief pathway by which bacteria evolve resistance against phage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial evolution.

claim: The best characterized phage resistance mutations involve alterations on cell surface receptor molecules that mediate phage attachment.
source: To date, the best characterized phage resistance mutations involve alterations on cell surface receptor molecules that mediate phage attachment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phage resistance mechanisms.

claim: In Escherichia coli, mutations in the cell-wall protein LamB confer resistance against lambda phage infection.
source: For example, in Escherichia coli, mutations in the cell-wall protein LamB confer resistance against lambda phage infection, while in S. aureus, mutations that modify wall teichoic acid (WTA) have been shown to limit phage infection (Gerlach et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The example is supported by citations to Gerlach et al., 2018 and Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: In S. aureus, mutations that modify wall teichoic acid (WTA) have been shown to limit phage infection.
source: For example, in Escherichia coli, mutations in the cell-wall protein LamB confer resistance against lambda phage infection, while in S. aureus, mutations that modify wall teichoic acid (WTA) have been shown to limit phage infection (Gerlach et al., 2018; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The example is supported by citations to Gerlach et al., 2018 and Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: A plethora of additional host mechanisms, including dedicated anti-phage defense systems, can impact the evolution of resistance against phage.
source: Complicating the picture, studies have revealed that a plethora of additional host mechanisms, including dedicated anti-phage defense systems, can impact the evolution of resistance against phage (Bernheim and Sorek, 2020; Maynard et al., 2010).
evidence: The complexity of resistance mechanisms is supported by citations to Bernheim and Sorek, 2020 and Maynard et al., 2010.

claim: A genetic trade-off is defined as an evolved trait that confers a fitness advantage against a particular selective pressure at the expense of reduced fitness against an unselected pressure.
source: A genetic trade-off is defined as an evolved trait that confers a fitness advantage against a particular selective pressure at the expense of reduced fitness against an unselected pressure.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: Trade-offs have been shown to occur between phage resistance and antibiotic resistance across many different species of bacteria.
source: Across many different species of bacteria, such trade-offs have been shown to occur between phage resistance and antibiotic resistance (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which illustrates the concept.

claim: In P. aeruginosa, infection by the phage OMKO1, which binds to the outer membrane protein M OprM of MexAB- and MexXY-OprM efflux pumps, drives the evolution of mutations in those genes, leading to the re-sensitization of phage-resistant P. aeruginosa mutants to antibiotics.
source: As an example, in P. aeruginosa, infection by the phage OMKO1, which binds to the outer membrane protein M OprM of MexAB- and MexXY-OprM efflux pumps, drives the evolution of mutations in those genes, leading to the re-sensitization of phage-resistant P. aeruginosa mutants to antibiotics (Kortright et al., 2019; Chan et al., 2016).
evidence: The example is supported by citations to Kortright et al., 2019 and Chan et al., 2016.

claim: Phage infection of S. aureus Newman can select for mutations in femA, which is a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the formation of the pentaglycine bridge of peptidoglycans in S. aureus.
source: For example, studies by Berryhill and colleagues demonstrated that phage infection of S. aureus Newman, an MSSA strain, can select for mutations in femA, which is a cytoplasmic enzyme that catalyzes the formation of the pentaglycine bridge of peptidoglycans in S. aureus (Berryhill et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Berryhill et al., 2021.

claim: femA maintains the integrity of the cell wall, which could be vital for WTA maturation and phage attachment.
source: Rather than serving as a direct phage receptor molecule, femA maintains the integrity of the cell wall, which in turn could be vital for WTA maturation and phage attachment (Azam and Tanji, 2019; Xia and Wolz, 2014).
evidence: The function of femA is supported by citations to Azam and Tanji, 2019 and Xia and Wolz, 2014.

claim: A consequence of femA mutations is increased sensitivity against antibiotics.
source: Interestingly, a consequence of these femA mutations is increased sensitivity against antibiotics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies about femA mutations.

claim: MRSA252 (USA200), MW2 (USA400), and LAC (USA300) are pathogenic isolates implicated in human disease and are used as representative examples for studying MRSA.
source: For our studies, we focused on three MRSA strains – MRSA252 (USA200), MW2 (USA400), and LAC (USA300). All three MRSA strains are pathogenic isolates implicated in human disease and are used as representative examples for studying MRSA (Voyich et al., 2005; Holden et al., 2004; Kobayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: The characterization of the strains is supported by citations to Voyich et al., 2005, Holden et al., 2004, and Kobayashi et al., 2011.

claim: ΦStaph1N belongs to the Kayvirus genus.
source: Of the phages tested, one phage, ΦStaph1N, which belongs to the Kayvirus genus, formed plaques on all three MRSA strains (Figure 1B; Xia and Wolz, 2014; Deghorain and Van Melderen, 2012).
evidence: The classification is supported by citations to Xia and Wolz, 2014 and Deghorain and Van Melderen, 2012, and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ΦStaph1N formed plaques on all three MRSA strains (MRSA252, MW2, and LAC).
source: Of the phages tested, one phage, ΦStaph1N, which belongs to the Kayvirus genus, formed plaques on all three MRSA strains (Figure 1B; Xia and Wolz, 2014; Deghorain and Van Melderen, 2012).
evidence: The plaquing activity is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ΦStaph1N infection was unable to eradicate MRSA cultures.
source: Yet, despite its ability to infect all three strains, ΦStaph1N infection was unable to eradicate MRSA cultures.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: MW2 and LAC displayed incomplete lysis in liquid culture at multiplicities of infection (MOIs) of 0.1 or lower.
source: Both MW2 and LAC displayed incomplete lysis in liquid culture at multiplicities of infection (MOIs) of 0.1 or lower (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The incomplete lysis is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Infected cultures of all three MRSA strains could recover back to high cell density after passaging one percent of the culture into fresh media following 24 hr of initial infection.
source: Furthermore, infected cultures of all three MRSA strains could recover back to high cell density after passaging one percent of the culture into fresh media following 24 hr of initial infection.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: ΦStaph1N was unable to form plaques on recovered MRSA cultures that survived in the initial ΦStaph1N infection.
source: Indeed, ΦStaph1N was unable to form plaques on recovered MRSA cultures that survived in the initial ΦStaph1N infection (Figure 1B).
evidence: The lack of plaquing on evolved cultures is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All three parental MRSA strains displayed high minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of ≥48 µg/mL against the β-lactams oxacillin (OXA), cefazolin (CEF), amoxicillin (AMX), and amoxicillin and clavulanic acid (AMX + CA).
source: As expected, all three strains displayed high minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of ≥48 µg/mL against the β-lactams oxacillin (OXA), cefazolin (CEF), amoxicillin (AMX), and amoxicillin and clavulanic acid (AMX + CA), visually indicated by their ability to form lawns surrounding antibiotic strips (Figure 1C).
evidence: The MIC values are shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The parental MRSA strains were sensitive to vancomycin (VANC; MICs = 1.5 µg/mL).
source: The strains were sensitive to vancomycin (VANC; MICs = 1.5 µg/mL), which inhibits cell wall synthesis through a different mechanism than β-lactams.
evidence: The MIC value is stated in the text.

claim: Phage-resistant MRSA that survived ΦStaph1N infection displayed a strong reduction in resistance against OXA, CEF, and AMX + CA, with fold reductions in MIC between 10 and 1000-fold.
source: Strikingly, phage-resistant MRSA that survived ΦStaph1N infection displayed a strong reduction in resistance against OXA, CEF, and AMX + CA, with fold reductions in MIC between 10 and 1000-fold (Figure 1D); no change in MIC was observed with VANC or with AMX alone.
evidence: The MIC reductions are shown in Figure 1D.

claim: No change in MIC was observed with VANC or with AMX alone after ΦStaph1N infection.
source: Strikingly, phage-resistant MRSA that survived ΦStaph1N infection displayed a strong reduction in resistance against OXA, CEF, and AMX + CA, with fold reductions in MIC between 10 and 1000-fold (Figure 1D); no change in MIC was observed with VANC or with AMX alone.
evidence: The lack of change is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: For MRSA252, ΦStaph1N MOIs as low as 10–5 can still drive the loss of resistance against oxacillin.
source: For MRSA252, we still observed a~3-order of magnitude fold reduction of MIC at an MOI of 10–5.
evidence: The MIC reduction at low MOI is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: For MW2, the reduction of MIC was markedly decreased with lower phage levels, showing no significant loss at MOIs of 10–3 or lower.
source: With MW2, the reduction of MIC was markedly decreased with lower phage levels, showing no significant loss at MOIs of 10–3 or lower.
evidence: The MOI-dependent effect is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: For LAC, two replicates displayed a reduction of MIC by an order of magnitude at an MOI of 10–4, while the third replicate did not display any change.
source: For LAC, two replicates displayed a reduction of MIC by an order of magnitude at an MOI of 10–4, while the third replicate did not display any change.
evidence: The variable response is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: Evo2 is a mutant form of ΦStaph1N that evolved higher lytic activity.
source: We hypothesized that these clear plaques were caused by a mutant form of ΦStaph1N that evolved higher lytic activity. We isolated phage clones from these single plaques and tested their activity against MRSA. This mutant phage, which we called Evo2, plaques on LAC and MW2 strains with higher efficiency, displaying comparable plaquing to MRSA252 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The identification and characterization of Evo2 is described in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Evo2 plaques on LAC and MW2 strains with higher efficiency than ΦStaph1N, displaying comparable plaquing to MRSA252.
source: This mutant phage, which we called Evo2, plaques on LAC and MW2 strains with higher efficiency, displaying comparable plaquing to MRSA252 (Figure 2A).
evidence: The improved plaquing efficiency is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Evo2 exhibits lytic activity against MW2 and LAC even at an MOI of 10–4, a concentration at which ΦStaph1N does not show any detectable activity against the two strains.
source: In growth experiments, we further observed that Evo2 lyses MRSA cultures at lower MOIs compared to ΦStaph1N (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Evo2 exhibits lytic activity against MW2 and LAC even at an MOI of 10–4, a concentration at which ΦStaph1N does not show any detectable activity against the two strains.
evidence: The lytic activity at low MOI is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Evo2 has a single point mutation in ORF141 that induces a premature stop codon.
source: We sequenced the genome of Evo2 to determine the genetic mechanism driving this enhanced activity. We observed a single point mutation in ORF141 that induces a premature stop codon (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The mutation is identified through genome sequencing and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ORF141 is predicted to be a putative DNA binding protein with an HTH motif.
source: Sequence analysis with HHpred predicts ORF141 to be a putative DNA binding protein with an HTH motif (PDB: 2LVS, E-value: 2.5e-9).
evidence: The prediction is based on sequence analysis using HHpred.

claim: Infection by Evo2 reduced the MICs of the three MRSA strains against OXA, CEF, and AMX + CA, while MICs against AMX alone and VAN did not change significantly.
source: Similar to ΦStaph1N, infection by Evo2 reduced the MICs of the three MRSA strains against OXA, CEF, and AMX + CA, while MICs against AMX alone and VAN did not change significantly (Figure 2B).
evidence: The MIC reductions are shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Evo2-resistant LAC became sensitized to fosfomycin and daptomycin in some cases.
source: We found that the MICs of these antibiotics did not change significantly, with a few exceptions: in some cases, Evo2-resistant LAC became sensitized to fosfomycin and daptomycin; furthermore, one replicate of Evo2-resistant MRSA252 evolved sensitivity to teicoplanin.
evidence: The sensitization is shown in Table 2.

claim: One replicate of Evo2-resistant MRSA252 evolved sensitivity to teicoplanin.
source: We found that the MICs of these antibiotics did not change significantly, with a few exceptions: in some cases, Evo2-resistant LAC became sensitized to fosfomycin and daptomycin; furthermore, one replicate of Evo2-resistant MRSA252 evolved sensitivity to teicoplanin.
evidence: The sensitization is shown in Table 2.

claim: Evo2 displayed dramatic variation in the plaquing efficiency against 30 USA300 strains isolated between 2008 and 2011.
source: We observe dramatic variation in the plaquing efficiency of ΦStaph1N and the 30 strains, while Evo2 exhibited a higher plaquing efficiency in the majority of the 30 strains (Table 3).
evidence: The plaquing efficiency is shown in Table 3.

claim: After 15 independent challenges with Evo2, phage-resistant populations could not be recovered from ADL1, 5, 6, and 12.
source: Interestingly, after 15 independent challenges with Evo2, we were not able to recover phage-resistant populations from ADL1, 5, 6, and 12.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described.

claim: In the USA300 clinical isolates that developed Evo2 resistance, the OXA MIC was reduced between 10- and 100-fold after Evo2 infection.
source: In the rest of the strains, we observed that similarly to MRSA252, MW2, and LAC, the OXA MIC was reduced between 10- and 100-fold after Evo2 infection (Figure 2C).
evidence: The MIC reductions are shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Infection with ΦNM1γ6, a phage of the Dubowvirus genus, generated phage resistance in MRSA but did not produce a drop in β-lactam resistance.
source: While the recovered LAC cultures exhibited resistance against ΦΝΜ1γ6, they did not show a reduction in MIC against the panel of β-lactams (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that phage resistance caused by ΦΝΜ1γ6 is uncoupled from β-lactam resistance.
evidence: The lack of MIC reduction is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: SATA8505 is active against MRSA252, MW2, and LAC, and infection caused a rise of phage resistance.
source: SATA8505 is active against MRSA252, MW2, and LAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), and infection of the three strains caused a rise of phage resistance in MRSA252, MW2, and LAC.
evidence: The activity and resistance evolution are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cells resistant to SATA8505 showed a strong loss of oxacillin resistance.
source: Similar to ΦStaph1N and Evo2, cells resistant to SATA8505 showed a strong loss of oxacillin resistance (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The loss of resistance is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Each MRSA strain evolved distinct mutation profiles following phage infection.
source: We observed that each MRSA strain evolved distinct mutation profiles (Figure 3A).
evidence: The distinct mutation profiles are shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Irrespective of the strain and phage treatment, most mutations were predicted to be substitutions, followed by truncations.
source: Irrespective of the strain and phage treatment, most mutations were predicted to be substitutions, followed by truncations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The mutation types are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No mutations were observed in the SCCmec or blaZ loci in phage-treated MRSA strains.
source: One plausible hypothesis explaining the loss of β-lactam resistance is that phage infection selected for a defective SCCmec or blaZ. However, we did not observe any mutations in the two loci.
evidence: This is an observation from the genomic sequencing analysis.

claim: In MRSA252, both ΦStaph1N and Evo2 infection selected for frameshift or nonsense mutations in the femA gene that would inactivate the protein product.
source: In MRSA252, both ΦStaph1N and Evo2 infection were selected for frameshift or nonsense mutations in the femA gene that would inactivate the protein product.
evidence: The mutations are identified through genomic sequencing and shown in Figure 3A and Table 4.

claim: Deletions of femA have been shown to increase susceptibility to β-lactams even when PBP2a (encoded by mecA) is expressed.
source: Deletions of femA have been shown to increase susceptibility to β-lactams even when PBP2a (encoded by mecA) is expressed, thus providing a genetic mechanism for how some MRSA252 cells lose β-lactam resistance after phage selection (Maidhof et al., 1991; Srisuknimit et al., 2017).
evidence: The effect of femA deletions is supported by citations to Maidhof et al., 1991 and Srisuknimit et al., 2017.

claim: In MW2, mutations were found in two transcriptional regulators, mgrA and sarA.
source: In MW2, we found mutations in two transcriptional regulators, mgrA and sarA (Figure 3A, Table 4).
evidence: The mutations are shown in Figure 3A and Table 4.

claim: Both mgrA and sarA belong to the family of MarR (multiple antibiotic resistance regulator)/SarA (staphylococcal accessory regulator A) proteins, which regulate drug resistance and virulence in S. aureus.
source: Both mgrA and sarA belong to the family of MarR (multiple antibiotic resistance regulator)/SarA (staphylococcal accessory regulator A) proteins, which regulate drug resistance and virulence in S. aureus (Li et al., 2016; Zielinska et al., 2012; Crosby et al., 2016).
evidence: The function of mgrA and sarA is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016, Zielinska et al., 2012, and Crosby et al., 2016.

claim: For LAC, nonsense mutations were found in arlR, which is part of the arlRS two-component signaling system.
source: For LAC, we observed a third, distinct mutational pattern (Figure 3A). Of note, we found nonsense mutations in arlR, which is part of the arlRS two-component signaling system (Table 4).
evidence: The mutations are shown in Figure 3A and Table 4.

claim: The activity of arlRS has been implicated in S. aureus virulence, pathogenicity, and oxacillin resistance.
source: The activity of arlRS has been implicated in S. aureus virulence, pathogenicity, and oxacillin resistance (Bai et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: The function of arlRS is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2019 and Walker et al., 2013.

claim: Substitution mutations were observed in spoVG, which is a transcription factor regulating the expression of genes involved in a variety of functions, including cell wall metabolism.
source: Further, we observed substitution mutations in spoVG, which is a transcription factor regulating the expression of genes involved in a variety of functions, including cell wall metabolism (Table 4; Schulthess et al., 2011).
evidence: The mutations are shown in Table 4, and the function of spoVG is supported by citation to Schulthess et al., 2011.

claim: spoVG activates the expression of femA.
source: Indeed, spoVG activates the expression of femA (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The regulatory relationship is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: spoVG modulates β-lactam antibiotic resistance by modulating cell wall synthesis.
source: Studies have shown that spoVG modulates β-lactam antibiotic resistance by modulating cell wall synthesis (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: The function of spoVG is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Single knockout mutants of mgrA, sarA, and arlR alone are not sufficient to confer resistance to ΦStaph1N and Evo2.
source: We therefore tested if single knockout mutants of these genes alone are sufficient to confer resistance to ΦStaph1N and Evo2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). In MW2, the mgrA knockout resulted in a modest reduction in plaquing of Evo2 and ΦStaph1N. However, none of the remaining mutants in either the MW2 or LAC background conferred resistance.
evidence: The plaquing assays are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phage-treated MRSA evolved mutations in a variety of transcriptional regulators, some of which are known to affect MRSA virulence.
source: Our genomic analysis revealed that phage-treated MRSA evolved mutations in a variety of transcriptional regulators, some of which are known to affect MRSA virulence.
evidence: This is a summary of the genomic analysis results.

claim: Significant changes in gene expression were observed in both MW2 and LAC following Evo2 treatment.
source: We performed bulk RNA-seq experiments on MW2 and LAC strains that were treated with the phage Evo2 and compared their transcription profiles to those of untreated strains (Figure 4, Supplementary file 2). We observed significant changes in gene expression in both MW2 and LAC.
evidence: The differential expression is shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: No significant changes in the expression of genes in the SCCmec cassette or blaZ were observed in phage-treated MW2 and LAC.
source: Notably, mirroring the trend seen in the mutational data, we did not observe significant changes in the expression of genes in the SCCmec cassette or blaZ present in both MW2 and LAC.
evidence: This is an observation from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Deletions of arlRS and mgrA de-repress the extracellular matrix binding protein ebh, resulting in significantly higher expression levels of the gene.
source: For example, Horswill and colleagues have shown that deletions of arlRS and mgrA de-repress the extracellular matrix binding protein ebh, resulting in significantly higher expression levels of the gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies by Horswill and colleagues.

claim: Deletions of arlRS and mgrA increased the expression of urease genes involved in the urea TCA cycle.
source: In addition, these deletions also increased the expression of urease genes involved in the urea TCA cycle (Crosby et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: The effect on urease genes is supported by citations to Crosby et al., 2016 and Walker et al., 2013.

claim: Differential expression data from both MW2 and LAC displayed log2 fold changes of >7 for ebh and >3 for ureABCDEFG genes.
source: Aligning with our hypothesis, differential expression data from both MW2 and LAC displayed log2 fold changes of >7 for ebh and >3 for ureABCDEFG genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The fold changes are shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Both MW2 and LAC strongly upregulated several genes involved in cell wall maintenance, including lytN and fmhC.
source: Additionally, both MW2 and LAC strongly upregulated several genes involved in cell wall maintenance. These include lytN, which is a murein hydrolase involved in the cross-wall compartment of S. aureus, and fmhC, which, as described previously, incorporates Gly-Ser dipeptides into pentaglycine cross-bridges in the S. aureus peptidoglycan cell wall.
evidence: The upregulation is observed in the RNA-seq data.

claim: Overexpression of lytN has been shown to damage the cell wall, which in turn is alleviated by overexpression of fmhC.
source: Overexpression of lytN has been shown to damage the cell wall, which in turn is alleviated by overexpression of fmhC (Willing et al., 2020).
evidence: The relationship between lytN and fmhC is supported by citation to Willing et al., 2020.

claim: fmhC overexpression is linked to increased β-lactam sensitivity.
source: Interestingly, fmhC overexpression is linked to increased β-lactam sensitivity and thus may contribute to the loss of β-lactam resistance phenotypes we observed in the MRSA strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed upregulation of fmhC and its known function.

claim: MW2 and LAC downregulated numerous genes, many of which are known virulence factors, including genes in the ess locus, staphyloxanthin biosynthesis, and quorum sensing.
source: MW2 and LAC also downregulated numerous genes, many of which are known virulence factors. Both strains reduced transcript levels of genes in the locus of the type VII secretion system (ess locus), staphyloxanthin biosynthesis (crtM, crtN, crtP), and quorum sensing (e.g. agrA; Figure 4, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The downregulation is shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The ess locus, staphyloxanthin biosynthesis, and quorum sensing pathways have been shown to bolster the ability of S. aureus to establish infection and evade the host immune system.
source: Individually, these pathways have been shown to bolster the ability of S. aureus to establish infection and evade the host immune system (Cao et al., 2016; Clauditz et al., 2006; Yarwood and Schlievert, 2003).
evidence: The function of these pathways is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2016, Clauditz et al., 2006, and Yarwood and Schlievert, 2003.

claim: MW2 showed a significant increase in the virulence factor spa following phage treatment.
source: For example, MW2 saw a significant increase in the virulence factor spa, known to interfere with the host immune response and interface with other bacterial species.
evidence: The upregulation is observed in the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The presence of cell wall-bound Protein A has been shown to decrease phage absorption, likely by masking WTA.
source: The presence of cell wall-bound Protein A has also been shown to decrease phage absorption, likely by masking WTA (Moller et al., 2021).
evidence: The function of Protein A is supported by citation to Moller et al., 2021.

claim: In MW2, tarM, which adds α1,4-GlcNAc to WTA, was strongly up-regulated (log2 ratio = 6.63).
source: Further in MW2, we found that tarM, which adds α1,4-GlcNAc to WTA, was strongly up-regulated (log2 ratio = 6.63).
evidence: The upregulation is observed in the RNA-seq data.

claim: Elevated tarM and α1,4-GlcNAc-WTA can lead to phage resistance in MRSA.
source: This is in line with previous findings showing that elevated tarM and α1,4-GlcNAc-WTA can lead to phage resistance in MRSA.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: LAC showed an increase in the expression (log2 fold change >3.8) of the hemolytic cytotoxin genes lukD/E, which lyses host cells and targets neutrophils.
source: The LAC showed an increase in the expression (log2 fold change >3.8) of the hemolytic cytotoxin genes lukD/E, which lyses host cells and targets neutrophils (Reyes-Robles et al., 2013).
evidence: The upregulation is observed in the RNA-seq data, and the function of lukD/E is supported by citation to Reyes-Robles et al., 2013.

claim: Evo2 infection of MRSA252 resulted in a significant reduction in Crystal Violet absorption compared to the parental strain.
source: We found that Evo2 infection of MRSA252 resulted in a significant reduction in Crystal Violet absorption compared to the parental strain.
evidence: The biofilm reduction is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant difference in Crystal Violet absorption was observed between parental, mock- and phage-treated MW2 and LAC strains.
source: However, we show no significant difference in Crystal Violet absorption between parental, mock- and phage-treated MW2 and LAC strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The lack of difference is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parental MW2 and LAC colonies lysed rabbit blood cells on blood agar plates, producing distinct halos of clearance around the bacterial cells.
source: Parental MW2 and LAC colonies lysed rabbit blood cells on blood agar plates, producing distinct halos of clearance around the bacterial cells.
evidence: The hemolysis is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For untreated LAC, the total area of hemolysis was on average 3-fold larger than that of untreated MW2 (~210 mm2 vs ~70 mm2, respectively).
source: For untreated LAC, the total area of hemolysis was on average 3-fold larger than that of untreated MW2 (~210 mm2 vs ~70 mm2, respectively); with MRSA252, by contrast, lysis was not detected (Figure 5A).
evidence: The hemolysis areas are shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: With MRSA252, hemolysis was not detected.
source: For untreated LAC, the total area of hemolysis was on average 3-fold larger than that of untreated MW2 (~210 mm2 vs ~70 mm2, respectively); with MRSA252, by contrast, lysis was not detected (Figure 5A).
evidence: The lack of hemolysis is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Following treatment with ΦStaph1N, MW2 and LAC displayed a reduced area of hemolysis by four- to fivefold.
source: Following treatment with ΦStaph1N, we observed that MW2 and LAC displayed a reduced area of hemolysis by four- to fivefold.
evidence: The reduction in hemolysis is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For Evo2-treated LAC, loss of hemolysis was even more pronounced, with two of the replicates showing no detectable hemolysis.
source: However, for Evo2-treated LAC, loss of hemolysis was even more pronounced, with two of the replicates showing no detectable hemolysis.
evidence: The loss of hemolysis is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neither MW2 nor LAC showed a reduction in transcript expression of hla following phage treatment.
source: We note that neither MW2 nor LAC showed a reduction in transcript expression of hla.
evidence: This is an observation from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The loss of hemolysis could be driven by an inability of phage-evolved MRSA to secrete the toxin.
source: We posit that the loss of hemolysis could be driven by an inability of phage-evolved MRSA to secrete the toxin.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that hla expression did not change.

claim: Phage-treated MW2 and LAC displayed less clumping than the mock-treated or parental strain.
source: Indeed, phage-treated MW2 and LAC displayed less clumping than the mock-treated or parental strain.
evidence: The reduced clumping is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For MW2, ΦStaph1N infection resulted in a modest reduction in clumping, while Evo2 infection resulted in a reduction of approximately 3-fold.
source: For MW2, ΦStaph1N infection resulted in a modest reduction, while Evo2 infection resulted in a reduction of approximately 3-fold (Figure 5B).
evidence: The clumping reduction is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In LAC, both ΦStaph1N and Evo2 treatment resulted in comparable reductions of clumping in surviving cells.
source: In LAC, we found that both ΦStaph1N and Evo2 treatment resulted in comparable reductions of clumping in surviving cells.
evidence: The clumping reduction is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For MRSA252, cells grew at low levels of Evo2 phage (MOI of 0.01 or less) and oxacillin (<0.125 µg/mL) in checkerboard assays.
source: For MRSA252, cells grew at low levels of phage (MOI of 0.01 or less) and oxacillin (<0.125 µg/mL; Figure 6A).
evidence: The growth pattern is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LAC displayed greater sensitivity to Evo2, showing no detectable growth after 48 hr in the presence of phage, irrespective of the presence of oxacillin.
source: LAC displayed greater sensitivity, showing no detectable growth after 48 hr in the presence of phage, irrespective of the presence of oxacillin.
evidence: The lack of growth is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For MW2, cells showed limited growth at MOIs <1 and oxacillin levels <0.125 µg/mL in Evo2 checkerboard assays.
source: For MW2, cells showed limited growth at MOIs <1 and oxacillin levels <0.125 µg/mL.
evidence: The growth pattern is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In MRSA252, cells from E2 and F2 wells were resistant to Evo2 infection and exhibited a 1000-fold decrease in MIC against oxacillin.
source: In MRSA252, cells from E2 and F2 were resistant to Evo2 infection and exhibited a 1000-fold decrease in MIC against oxacillin.
evidence: The resistance and MIC reduction are shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In MW2, the six viable cultures from Evo2/oxacillin treatment exhibited Evo2 resistance and a 10- to 100-fold decrease in MIC.
source: Similarly, in MW2, the six viable cultures exhibited Evo2 resistance and a 10- to 100-fold decrease in MIC.
evidence: The resistance and MIC reduction are shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Neither MRSA252 nor LAC could grow in any ΦStaph1N/oxacillin combination in checkerboard assays.
source: We next analyzed how MRSA grew under ΦStaph1N/β-lactam combinations (Figure 6A, bottom row). Neither MRSA252 nor LAC could grow in any ΦStaph1N/oxacillin combination; MW2, by contrast, grew across under a wide range of ΦStaph1N/oxacillin combinations.
evidence: The lack of growth is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When ΦStaph1N-infected MW2 was treated with high (16 µg/mL) levels of oxacillin, recovered cells showed no reduction in MIC against oxacillin.
source: When ΦStaph1N-infected MW2 was treated with high (16 µg/mL) levels of oxacillin, recovered cells (wells D11 and E11) showed no reduction in MIC against oxacillin (Figure 6C).
evidence: The lack of MIC reduction is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When ΦStaph1N-infected MW2 was co-treated with low levels (<0.125 µg/mL) of oxacillin, recovered cells displayed strong phage resistance and a 100-fold reduction in oxacillin resistance.
source: However, when ΦStaph1N-infected MW2 was co-treated with low levels (<0.125 µg/mL) of oxacillin, recovered cells (C3) displayed strong phage resistance and a 100-fold reduction in oxacillin resistance, mirroring phenotypes observed in the single phage treatment experiments.
evidence: The resistance and MIC reduction are shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Infection by certain staphylococcal phages sensitizes different strains of MRSA to β-lactams.
source: Here, we report the discovery that infection by certain staphylococcal phages sensitizes different strains of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) to β-lactams, a class of antibiotics against which MRSA is typically resistant.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: MRSA cells that survive infection by these phages display significant reductions in minimal inhibitory concentration against different β-lactams compared to uninfected bacteria.
source: MRSA cells that survive infection by these phages display significant reductions in minimal inhibitory concentration against different β-lactams compared to uninfected bacteria.
evidence: This is a summary of the MIC reduction findings shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Phage-treated MRSA exhibited attenuated virulence phenotypes in the form of reduced hemolysis and clumping.
source: Phage-treated MRSA exhibited attenuated virulence phenotypes in the form of reduced hemolysis and clumping.
evidence: This is a summary of the virulence phenotype findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Despite sharing similar phenotypes, whole-sequencing analysis revealed that the different MRSA strains evolved unique genetic profiles during infection.
source: Despite sharing similar phenotypes, whole-sequencing analysis revealed that the different MRSA strains evolved unique genetic profiles during infection.
evidence: This is a summary of the genomic sequencing findings shown in Figure 3.
